_about: The dashboard To-Do feed. Refreshed at every Rule 8 checkpoint alongside the session handoff — this is the handoff distilled into plain language for the 📋 button on every tab. Split For Sam (curation / decisions only a human makes) and For Fable (engineering, the next session picks up).
_as_of: 2026-08-24 · SkyView (Session 187) went to the Common Course Reference. Sam asked for an interactive graph view because opening the CCR is overwhelming, and named the real goal: get 142,000 local college courses down to about 2,500 common ones. The most important thing we found is arithmetic, not design. If we worked the entire merge queue and got every single decision right, we would still end up with about 36,000 courses — fourteen times too many. Merging can only compare courses that already exist. The only thing that reaches the goal is packaging: deciding what the catalog should contain and mapping courses into it, which is exactly what the ESL plan does. The second thing: the CCR is not 17,000 rows of work, it is 6,056 decisions, and 97% of them involve twelve courses or fewer. Automotive Technology is 57 decisions. Welding is 35. A sitting each. There is now a prototype you can click that shows it that way, and the ability to drag a course to where it belongs turned out to have been built a year ago and never once used.
_status: The CCR now has an interface to react to and a number that should steer it. Nothing has been written to the curation data — everything this run was read-only or a drawing. Two decisions are yours before the first fold can happen: what to call the three ESL courses everything folds into, and a spot-check of the 794 courses that were put in 'Beginning' simply because their title did not say a level. Both are visible in the prototype. Separately, we found a real over-merge: five different Orange Coast College courses sitting under one row, and the same shape appears on 3,320 rows across the whole reference.

items.text: Name the three ESL courses that everything folds into. Right now 1,846 ESL courses are sorted into Beginning, Intermediate and Advanced — but those three destination courses do not actually exist yet, so nothing can move until they have names. This does not renumber anything or touch any college's records. Open the prototype and press 'See the proposal'.

Spot-check the Beginning pile. 794 of the 1,110 courses landing in Beginning got there only because their title did not mention a level, so we assumed the lowest one — which is the safe guess but often the wrong one. The prototype lists them with the uncertain ones first and says in plain words why each was put where it was.

Have a look at the CCR prototype and tell us what is wrong with it. The main thing to judge: is one decision at a time the right size to work in, or do you want to see a whole subject at once? That answer decides what we build next.

One row to look at: five different Orange Coast College courses — Reading and Vocabulary, Sentence Structure, Spelling, Pronunciation and Grammar — are all filed as one course, under the name of just one of them. A college does not teach the same course under five different numbers, so this is wrong. 3,320 rows across the reference have that same shape.

Fourteen of the 22 transfer-level ESL courses were already merged away by automation before anyone reviewed them. These are the ones that award real transferable credit, so they were supposed to be confirmed one at a time. Eight are still standing. Worth deciding whether the others should be put back — it is one row each to undo.

Build the whole-universe view Sam asked for: every course on one canvas, with keyword search zooming to a cluster. It has to be a precomputed layout drawn on canvas with labels appearing as you zoom in — a map, not a live force graph, which would be an unreadable hairball at 17,000 nodes. Wait until Sam has judged the single-decision view first.

Add the over-merge detector to the auditor: flag any course row where every college listed is the same college but the course numbers differ. 3,320 rows qualify. It must only flag, never un-merge on its own — some are legitimate, like independent-study courses.

Half the CCR queue — 3,001 decisions covering 8,065 courses — has no subject assigned at all, so it cannot be merged until someone says what subject each belongs to. That is a different job from merging and needs its own screen.
The docs index has grown to six and a half times its size budget, mostly one very long line per knowledge-base note. Worth a compaction pass so the file stays usable.

Settle the noncredit minimum — it is the last open number on the funding tab. At the $50,000 you set, 30 of the 33 noncredit institutions land exactly on it and an institution has to reach 3,909 noncredit FTES before growing earns it anything extra. At $25,000 it was 27 of 33 and 3,022 FTES. So the current setting rewards getting into the lane and pays very little for growing inside it. If that is what you want, nothing needs to change. If you wanted growth to pay, lowering the minimum is the lever — raising the set-aside on its own makes it more floor-bound, not less. The box on the tab and the explainer page both show the break-even figure live, so you can move the dial and watch it.

Your question about splitting P1 into three metrics (landing page, student portal, batch upload). Short answer: get the breakdown first, split later if the data says to. Splitting it into three priorities would split the MONEY three ways — each would get its own target and its own cap, so a college doing everything through its landing page could no longer make up the difference elsewhere. That is a real change: it would require colleges to work all three routes rather than reach one total. Also, batch upload is not really the same thing as the other two — those are students arriving, that is an administrative import — so it is the one worth treating differently whatever you decide. Recommendation: when the data lands next week we show the three origins as a breakdown on the existing P1, in the drill-in and the export. You then have the evidence, and splitting later is a settings change, not a rebuild.

Move Sierra's Anthropic billing to the corporate account when you can. She went dark twice in two days on the personal balance — 2026-08-21 and again overnight — and each outage takes down every place she appears at once: the public page, the COBI tab, the Fact Sheet drawer, map.rccd.edu, the college landing pages and the vendor iframe. A student who arrives in that window gets nothing and files no complaint, so the outage cannot report itself. There is now an automatic check every three hours that will open a GitHub issue and close it on recovery, so you will hear about the next one — but it tells you after the fact, it does not prevent it.

Trial Haiku 4.5 against the smoke suite. It is a third of Sonnet's price both directions and stacks with the caching we just shipped rather than competing with it. ONE of the two concerns is now closed: her biggest measured question used about 23,000 tokens against Haiku's 200,000 limit, a 9x margin, so capacity is not the obstacle — that came free from the deploy telemetry. What is left is only whether a smaller model keeps the careful bits: the 'not every recommendation should be applied' caveat, 'showing 9 of 261' rather than implying that is all of them, not calling an absent college zero. Several smoke assertions test exactly those. Run it, diff the failures, report — do not switch quietly.

MAP needs to give us two college IDs. You ruled that Calbright and LAUNCH each have two entities — one credit, one noncredit. The noncredit halves already have IDs; the credit halves ("Calbright College Credit" and "Launch Apprenticeship Non-Credit") have none anywhere we can see, and MAP is the only system allowed to assign one. We deliberately did NOT make one up, because a fake ID would look exactly like a real one to every other system. They show as "awaiting MAP ID" on the College Identity tab. Once MAP supplies them, they fold in with no code change.
